claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid solutions with homogeneous elemental distributions and low noble-metal content.
Substitution with a chemically similar element of different atomic radius can modulate atomic-size mismatch while maintaining near-equiatomic composition.
Greater atomic-size mismatch induces greater lattice distortion and local strain fields.
Increased lattice distortion raises the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
A higher diffusion activation energy reduces atomic mobility at elevated temperature.
Reduced atomic mobility inhibits phase separation.
Reduced atomic mobility inhibits chemical ordering or atomic reordering.
Nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion will have better high-temperature structural stability than baseline nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch.
Nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion will have better high-temperature chemical stability than baseline nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch.
Modified nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion will exhibit slower diffusion than baseline nanoparticles.
Modified nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure longer during high-temperature exposure than baseline nanoparticles.
The proposed effects are expected to be observable only within the specified high-temperature operational regimes.
Below a critical atomic-size-difference threshold, effects on diffusion activation energy and phase stability may be negligible.
The critical atomic-radius difference required to alter diffusion kinetics significantly is not established.
